variants.name: const data members with const accessors (final after construction)
variants.idiom_name: const data member initialized in the constructor initializer list
variants.implementation_notes: The direct C++ realization of 'final after construction': declare the state as `const` data members (or one `const` member of a small nested struct) and initialize them in the constructor's member-initializer list, so every later assignment - including one in a subclass's method - is ill-formed, while `const` member functions return the values. The two-class split collapses into a const-qualified member, which is why the classic holder object is only worth writing when several fields must be validated and frozen as a unit. Choose this form for value types that are cheap to copy and never reassigned; remember that a const member removes assignment and therefore constrains how the type can be stored and moved.
pitfalls: A `const` data member deletes the implicit copy assignment and blocks moves into containers that require assignability; hold the state in a const-qualified nested struct or hand out accessors instead.
A `const` pointer or reference member still lets callers mutate the pointee, so return copies or const references to immutable-by-type data.
Aggregate initialization and `= default` copy semantics stop working once a const member exists, which quietly changes how the type can be serialized, swapped or sorted.

variants.name: pimpl (opaque pointer) hiding the read-only implementation
variants.implementation_notes: Hide the representation behind a pointer to a forward-declared `struct impl` that is defined only in the .cpp file: private data leaves the header, the class keeps nothing but its public API, and every read goes through the pointer - the compiler-firewall form of the pattern, chosen when ABI stability or build-time decoupling matters. The indirection does not itself forbid writes, so make the members of `impl` const (or wrap the pointer in a const-propagating smart pointer) and expose only const accessors. Prefer it over an inline implementation in widely included headers and shared libraries; skip it in small, hot value types where the extra allocation dominates.
pitfalls: `std::unique_ptr` does not propagate constness: a `const` member function still obtains a mutable `impl&`, so writes through the pimpl compile unless the pointer is wrapped (propagate_const) or accessors return const references.
Special members must be declared and defined out of line where `impl` is complete, and the user-declared destructor suppresses the implicit move operations unless they are defaulted explicitly.
One extra allocation per object plus one indirection per access is visible in small, frequently created value types and defeats inlining outside LTO builds.
